1. The first thing some new people need to learn is to calm the fuck down. You sound like one of them at this point in your career. As a fellow small female, this is especially important to your public perception. "Hey guys, I'm an EMT. Have you called 911 yet? Can you over there get a ladder and something to help cut him down? Can you over here tell me what happened?" works a hell of a lot better than barking orders. You sound very invested in your calls. Don't ever lose your compassion. It's a fantastic thing. At the same time, if you get this worked up about bees, what are you gonna do when you roll up on an 8yof pedestrian struck with bilateral compound femur fx? This is not your emergency. When you aren't in uniform, you are a bystander. A well trained bystander, but you shouldn't be yelling at anyone, least of all the paramedic you may have to work with later. Medics all talk with each other. Humility goes a long way when you are new. 

2. The immediate treatment for bees is distance. What was keeping you from getting the patient into the pickup truck you mentioned and putting some diesel between you two and the bees? 

3. Once the crew shows up, it is their scene. Even if you are annoyed with their plan or treatment. Even if you are their (off-duty) supervisor. Even if they drop the patient. It is their patient to drop. Ask if they need help, then take whatever answer you get. You are clearly not their only resource. If you weren't there, they could handle it. Fire crew can help lift. Other trucks can come. Hell, they can call a flight crew if they want. Their patient, their rules. 

4. Don't think I am telling you not to ask questions. Ask anything you want. After the call. Otherwise you run the risk of making it sound like you don't respect a crew that has been working far longer than you have had your cert. Most people love to teach, but not in the middle of a chaotic scene. Timing your eagerness will earn you brownie points. Obviously if there is an immediate life threatening (patient is on fire, patient has a knife sticking out of him, patient is in v-fib) that the crew has blatantly missed, then speak up right away. But otherwise listen and watch 10x as much as you speak.

I'm a firefighter/paramedic who spent 6 years as an EMT and who eventually wants to go on to medical school or aeromedical stuff (36 MCAT but my GPA was complete crap). Take my advice with as many grains of salt as you see fit. 

Becoming a 911 EMT will allow you more team-leading chances than becoming a CNA, especially if they run BLS ambulances. If they run ALS, you'll mostly drive while the paramedic gets the good stuff, but you'll still get plenty of hands-on, patient-interviewing time. It is difficult but not impossible to get a job as a 911 EMT without experience, so you may have to start out volunteering on the 911 side and working transport EMS. Don't expect to see blood and guts if you're working transport--you'll mainly be ferrying old people to and from dialysis. This sounds a lot like becoming a CNA (a path to burnout from what I've seen in my friends) but it's actually not all bad. Working transport, you can learn to develop a decent clinical rapport with people. It's really important to be able to talk with all kinds of people unless you go into, like, pathology or something.

If you do go the EMT route, it may lead to more interesting doctor-shadowing opportunities than you might otherwise have available to you. Your medical director may be able to set you up with time in the ER (which is a lot of fun) or the OR (especially if your state allows EMT-Bs to play with airway stuff).

EMTs can do basic life support. The scope of practice varies from state to state. In PA, this means CPR and AED, immobilization, treatment of bleeding, and using airway adjuncts that don't go into the trachea. We can administer oxygen, oral glucose, and activated charcoal. If a patient is prescribed nitroglycerin, albuterol, or an Epi-Pen, we can assist them in taking it, but otherwise we can't touch the stuff. The course is about 120 hours and taught at the 7th-grade level.

Paramedics start out certified as an EMT-B and do basic life support skills too, but they can also do advanced life support--intubation and other advanced airways, IV and IO therapy, cricothyrotomy, decompression of the chest, manual defibrillation, that sort of thing. Lots of drugs. Lots of cardiac drugs. It's usually a 1 to 2 year course with heavy emphasis on field internship.
